segments.text: Zerops deploys exactly what you tell it. Nobody tells it everything — your code picks up a search engine on a Tuesday, and the project never hears about it.

Three times building this, the platform returned two hundred and did nothing. Import variables ignored. An autoscaling body one level too shallow — accepted, finished, applied to nothing. You only catch those by reading the value back.
So Notch holds your repo against your live account, proves every gap with a line of code, and lets agents argue about the fix.
It starts with a Zerops access token, checked by a real API call rather than by the shape of the string. Memory only. Never on disk, never logged, only ever shown redacted.
This is the board. Real nodes on a real canvas — drag them, pan, zoom, fit. The arrangement is remembered per project, so your layout survives a rescan.

Click a service and everything more than one hop away dims. That is what a diagram is for: what else breaks if this goes down. The runtime touches everything except the two services the platform runs for itself.
You can place a service by hand. It joins the same plan the scanner feeds, and it lands dashed, because nothing is created until you confirm the import file.
Now point it at a repository. Notch reads the manifests and compares them against what the project actually runs. Six services missing, drawn inside the project that is missing them.
Every finding cites the line that produced it. Qdrant, because the code imports the Qdrant client. Object storage, because it imports the S3 SDK. Nothing is claimed that cannot point at a file.
It reads the other direction too — variables the app expects that this project does not define. The database exists, and the code still cannot reach it.

And the opposite problem: a credential already in your repository. Only files git tracks, because a dot env that git ignores is where it belongs. Notice what is not on screen. A finding is a file, a line, and a kind — never the secret itself.
Describe what you are building. An agent picks the services from what this account can actually create.

The interesting half is what it turned down. Typesense over Meilisearch, because chat search is filter first — scope every query to your rooms or it leaks messages. And no to Qdrant, because finding messages that mean something similar is not finding the message where Ana said deploy.
Now the part that is not a linter. Three agents watch a live service and argue about resizing it. Disarmed, with a ceiling, because containers cost money.
Notch puts real traffic through the deployed URL and measures what comes back, then reads the containers and the policy from the platform.

Each agent argues one side. Capacity sees zero failures across twenty-four requests and says there is no evidence the container is struggling. Cost will not pay for capacity it cannot prove is needed. Reliability points out that one container is a single point of failure. Two of three have to agree, and a tie holds.
Armed, it makes the call, then reads the range back — because two hundred from this endpoint means the request was well formed and nothing more.
The receipts. Every request Notch made to Zerops, with status and timing, and the ones that changed something marked as writes. A search is a read, even though Zerops does it with a POST.
It will hold two projects against each other and show where staging and production drifted. Matched by service type, not by hostname.
Twenty-four calls this session, and not one of them changed your account. The panel voted to hold, so Notch held. When it does write, it lands right here with its status.
All of it real. A live URL answering two hundred, two hundred and eighty seven tests, every finding traceable to a line. Notch tells you what you forgot, before the pull request merges.
